title: Connected EF1 Allocations and Pareto Optimality Are Incompatible for Discrete Chores on a Path
abstract: When indivisible chores are arranged on a path and agents must receive connected bundles, does there always exist an allocation that is envy-free up to one chore (EF1) and Pareto optimal among connected allocations? In discrete chore cutting, connected EF1 allocations are known to exist for monotone costs, and EF1 and Pareto optimality are compatible when bundles need not be connected. We answer this question negatively. With three agents and five chores having additive, strictly positive costs, every connected EF1 allocation is Pareto-dominated by another connected allocation. Specifically, when agent 0 has cost vector $(4,2,1,2,2)$ and agents 1 and 2 each have cost vector $(1,4,1,2,2)$, each of the 12 connected EF1 allocations is Pareto-dominated by a connected allocation with cost vector $(5,1,2)$, $(2,1,5)$, or $(2,5,1)$. Consequently, the stronger condition EF1outer is also incompatible with connected Pareto optimality. This counterexample is formalized and checked in Lean as `connected_ef1_po_chores_incompatible`.
introduction:
In the fair division of indivisible chores among agents, two standard desiderata are fairness and economic efficiency. When chores are arranged along a path, connectivity is often required: each agent must receive a contiguous bundle of chores (an interval along the path). An allocation is envy-free up to one chore (EF1) if, whenever an agent envies another agent, the envy can be eliminated by removing some single chore from the envying agent's own bundle. Pareto optimality is evaluated with respect to connected allocations: an allocation is Pareto optimal if no other connected allocation gives every agent at most as much cost and at least one agent strictly less cost.

Without the connectivity requirement, EF1 and Pareto optimality are compatible for additive chores. Furthermore, in the connected setting, it was established in arXiv:2609.32545 that connected EF1 allocations—and even allocations satisfying the stronger condition EF1outer—always exist for agents with monotone cost functions. However, the compatibility of fairness and efficiency in the connected setting remained open. In Section 4 (Conclusion) of arXiv:2609.32545, the question was raised whether EF1 and Pareto optimality are compatible in the discrete chores division setting when allocations are restricted to connected bundles on a path.

This post presents a negative answer to this question. For additive, strictly positive costs, connected EF1 allocations and connected Pareto optimal allocations can be incompatible. Specifically, there exists an instance with three agents and five chores on a path where each connected EF1 allocation is Pareto-dominated by another connected allocation. Because the EF1outer condition implies EF1, this instance also establishes that EF1outer and Pareto optimality are incompatible for connected chores. The theorem is formalized and verified in Lean as `connected_ef1_po_chores_incompatible`.
result:
The main theorem establishes that fairness and efficiency can be incompatible for connected chore allocation on a path:

Theorem (`connected_ef1_po_chores_incompatible`). There exists a cost profile $c : \{0,1,2\} \times \{0,1,2,3,4\} \to \mathbb{R}$ with strictly positive costs $c(i, e) > 0$ for all agents $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ and chores $e \in \{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}$ such that no allocation $\sigma : \{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\} \to \{0, 1, 2\}$ is simultaneously connected (`is_connected_allocation`), envy-free up to one chore (`is_ef1_chores`), and Pareto optimal among connected allocations (`is_connected_po_chores`).

The Lean statement asserts the existence of a strictly positive cost function $c : \text{Fin } 3 \to \text{Fin } 5 \to \mathbb{R}$ such that there does not exist any chore assignment $\sigma : \text{Fin } 5 \to \text{Fin } 3$ satisfying `is_connected_allocation σ`, `is_ef1_chores c σ`, and `is_connected_po_chores c σ`.

In the counterexample instance, the cost vectors across the five path-ordered chores $0, 1, 2, 3, 4$ are:

- $c(0, \cdot) = (4, 2, 1, 2, 2)$ for agent 0,
- $c(1, \cdot) = (1, 4, 1, 2, 2)$ for agent 1,
- $c(2, \cdot) = (1, 4, 1, 2, 2)$ for agent 2.

Among all connected allocations of the five chores to the three agents, exactly 12 allocations satisfy the EF1 condition. Each of these 12 allocations is Pareto-dominated by a connected allocation whose agent cost vector is $(5, 1, 2)$, $(2, 1, 5)$, or $(2, 5, 1)$.

Since the EF1outer condition implies EF1, this instance also shows that EF1outer and Pareto optimality among connected allocations are incompatible.
proof:
The proof proceeds by analyzing the instance with three agents and five chores ordered on a path, with cost function $c : \text{Fin } 3 \to \text{Fin } 5 \to \mathbb{R}$ given by $c(0, \cdot) = (4, 2, 1, 2, 2)$ and $c(1, \cdot) = c(2, \cdot) = (1, 4, 1, 2, 2)$. Each cost $c(i, e)$ is strictly positive.

For an allocation $\sigma : \text{Fin } 5 \to \text{Fin } 3$, the bundle of agent $i$ is defined by `bundle_of` as the set of items assigned to $i$. The allocation satisfies `is_connected_allocation` if each agent's bundle forms a connected subpath of the path $\{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}$. Under `additive_valuation`, the total cost to agent $i$ is the sum of $c(i, e)$ over all chores $e$ in $i$'s bundle.

The condition `is_ef1_chores` requires that for every pair of agents $i$ and $j$, if agent $i$ envies agent $j$ under $i$'s cost function, there exists some chore in $i$'s bundle whose removal eliminates the envy. The condition `is_connected_po_chores` specifies that an allocation is Pareto optimal among connected allocations if no other connected allocation yields weakly smaller costs for all agents and a strictly smaller cost for at least one agent.

The proof verifies that among all connected allocations of the five chores to the three agents, exactly 12 allocations satisfy `is_ef1_chores`. For each of these 12 allocations, the proof demonstrates that it fails `is_connected_po_chores` by exhibiting an explicit connected allocation that Pareto-dominates it:

- Each candidate allocation is Pareto-dominated by a connected allocation whose cost vector across agents $(0, 1, 2)$ is either $(5, 1, 2)$, $(2, 1, 5)$, or $(2, 5, 1)$.
- In each case, the dominating allocation is verified to satisfy `is_connected_allocation`, and its cost vector is strictly smaller in at least one coordinate and no larger in any coordinate.

Since every connected allocation either fails `is_ef1_chores` or is Pareto-dominated by another connected allocation, no connected allocation can be simultaneously EF1 and Pareto optimal. This establishes `connected_ef1_po_chores_incompatible`.
discussion:
The theorem provides a counterexample that refutes the question posed in Section 4 of arXiv:2609.32545, establishing that connected EF1 allocations and Pareto optimality among connected allocations are not always compatible.

This incompatibility highlights a sharp contrast between connected and unconnected chore division:

- Without connectivity constraints, EF1 and Pareto optimality are compatible for additive chores.
- In the connected chore setting, connected EF1 allocations (and even EF1outer allocations) are guaranteed to exist for monotone costs according to arXiv:2609.32545, but demanding Pareto optimality among connected allocations makes the two properties incompatible.
- Because EF1outer implies EF1, the counterexample simultaneously rules out the compatibility of connected EF1outer allocations with connected Pareto optimality.

The counterexample settles the question as posed in arXiv:2609.32545 in the negative using an instance with three agents and five chores with additive, strictly positive costs.
